pages.text: The class group chat was buzzing. Someone had posted a story about Lordina: that she had cheated in a test, that she had been sent out of class, that she cried in the toilet. None of it came with proof. Messages piled on messages. Evelyn read them on her phone at home, and her thumb hovered over the forward button. “Everyone is sharing it,” she thought.

Someone had posted a story about Lordina: that she had cheated in a test, that she had been sent out of class, that she cried in the toilet.
None of it came with proof.
Messages piled on messages.
Evelyn read them on her phone at home, and her thumb hovered over the forward button.
“Everyone is sharing it,” she thought.
pages.alt: A girl at home holds a phone with a glowing screen of speech bubbles, her thumb above a button.

pages.text: Madam Torgbor, the ICT teacher, had once taught the class a rule: “Before you post, pause for ten seconds and ask three questions. Is it true? Is it kind? Is it necessary?” Evelyn counted. Is it true? She had no idea. Is it kind? She almost laughed at that one. Is it necessary? Not at all. She lowered her phone.

pages.text: The next day, Lordina sat alone at her desk and barely spoke. Her eyes were red. Evelyn’s stomach dropped. “She has seen it,” she thought. A classmate whispered, “Did you read the chat? It is so funny.” Evelyn shook her head. “It is not funny,” she said quietly. “It is not even true. Somebody made it up.”

pages.alt: A girl sits alone at a desk looking sad while two classmates whisper behind her.

pages.text: Madam Torgbor had a lesson that day on the digital footprint. “Everything you post leaves a trace,” she said. “A screenshot can be saved by anyone, even if you delete the message. A rumour can follow a person for years. Hurtful posts can break school rules and, in serious cases, may break the law. And the person who forwards it is part of the harm, not just the person who started it.”

pages.text: After class, Evelyn walked to Lordina’s desk. “I saw the rumour,” she said. “I did not share it, and I do not believe it. I am sorry it happened.” Lordina’s eyes filled again. “Thank you,” she whispered. “I thought everyone hated me.” Evelyn sat beside her. “Not everyone,” she said. “Let us tell Madam Torgbor together.”

pages.text: Madam Torgbor listened and kept the girls’ names private. She asked the class to stop the chat and delete the rumour, and she met the head teacher and the parents. A few students who had joked in the chat apologised. “Rules about phones differ from school to school,” she said, “but kindness is the same everywhere.” Evelyn felt something heavy lift off her chest.

pages.text: Evelyn wrote to Lordina, with her address and the date at the top. “House 8, Mill Road, Kpando. 4th April, 2027. Dear Lordina, I hope you are feeling better. I am sorry that you were hurt by the messages in the class chat. I should have spoken up sooner, and I am sorry I did not. I admire how strong you have been. Please let me know if there is anything I can do to help. Your friend, Evelyn.”

Dear Lordina, I hope you are feeling better.
I am sorry that you were hurt by the messages in the class chat.
I should have spoken up sooner, and I am sorry I did not.
I admire how strong you have been.
Please let me know if there is anything I can do to help.
Your friend, Evelyn.”
pages.alt: A girl writes an apology letter with a phone switched off beside her.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: an apology letter should be sincere, specific and written in full words. Evelyn named what had happened and what she would do differently. She did not write “sorry” on its own, and she did not use a chat shortcut such as “sry”. Real feelings need real words. The end.
